title: Creation's song
hook: the psalm of wild goats, lions and the sea (Psalm 104)
tomorrow: the book of Psalms ends on one word. which one?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the wings of the morning, and a hand waiting at the far edge of the sea. Today, the same sea, and what swims in it.
screen: `WINGS OF THE MORNING.` → `WHAT SWIMS IN THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Nature documentaries have a narrator who sounds like he loves the animals more than the people. Psalm 104 has that voice, long before any camera. "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies." "The young lions roar after their prey, and seek their meat from God." And out on the water: "There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein." So, yesterday's question: why goats, lions and a sea monster at play? Because the psalm is asking what the world is for. And readers have argued about the answer.
screen: `A NARRATOR WHO LOVES THE ANIMALS.` → `GOATS, LIONS, LEVIATHAN.` → `WHAT IS THE WORLD FOR?`

segments.voice: Psalm 104 sings creation, and in the middle it bursts out: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches." Manifold: many, and many kinds. Now the argument, inside the same Bible. One reading starts in Genesis, where God blesses the first humans and tells them to "have dominion over the fish of the sea," the birds and every living thing. On this reading, people are set over creation, to use it with God's blessing. Its best case: Genesis says so plainly, and its readers see farming, medicine and cities as people taking that charge seriously. The other reading points to the next chapter, where the man is put in the garden "to dress it and to keep it," and then to this psalm. Here the goats get their hills, the lions get their food from God, and the leviathan is made to play, useful to no one. People appear as one creature among many: "Man goeth forth unto his work and to his labour until the evening," after the lions have had the night. Its best case: the world has worth before it's useful to us. Jewish and Christian teachers have argued both, and some join them: rule, yes, but a ruler who answers to the maker for the land. One to tell a friend: in Jewish prayer, Psalm 104 is said at the new month.
screen: `HOW MANIFOLD ARE THY WORKS!` · `DOMINION: SET OVER CREATION.` · `KEEP IT: A WORLD WITH ITS OWN WORTH.` · `A RULER WHO ANSWERS FOR IT.` · then, large: `MANIFOLD WORKS.`

segments.voice: Say out loud the names of five creatures you've seen this week: a pigeon, a neighbor's dog, the spider in the corner, anything that moves. After each name, pause for one breath, as if it were a line in the psalm. Then sit with the list.
Creation's song: Psalm 104, where goats, lions, ships and the leviathan all get a verse, and the earth is full of riches.
Pocket this one: manifold works, each with its own place in the song. Three psalms down this week.

howItsDone: In Jewish prayer, Psalm 104 (Barchi nafshi) is said on the new month; Jewish and Christian teachers read it beside Genesis 1 and 2 when they ask how people should treat the earth.

chat.meaning: Genesis gives dominion; Genesis 2 says dress and keep it; Psalm 104 gives wild creatures their own places. Both readings live inside the tradition.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3: written new in recipe v3 (shape debate). Two readings inside the Jewish and Christian tradition, each given its best case: dominion (Genesis 1:28) and keeping (Genesis 2:15, Psalm 104). No side is ranked; 'some join them' (rule as answerable stewardship) is hedged.
KJV quotations (Psalm 104:18, 21, 23, 24, 26; Genesis 1:28; 2:15): check word for word. 'Labour' is KJV spelling inside quotation marks.

'People appear as one creature among many … after the lions have had the night' paraphrases Psalm 104:20–23; the psalm does mention people elsewhere (vv. 14–15), so no 'never mentions people' claim is made.
'In Jewish prayer, Psalm 104 is said at the new month' (Barchi nafshi on Rosh Chodesh): confirm with a Jewish Keeper; some communities also say it on winter Sabbath afternoons (not stated).
Story rule: the 'story' here is the psalm's own retelling of creation and the Genesis creation accounts it is read beside; a Keeper may prefer adding the waters fleeing at God's rebuke (104:6–9).
